html:
Gouy balance
Measuring magnetic susceptibility: a sample hangs in the gap of an electromagnet and its apparent mass changes when the field is switched on.
Guided demo
Field lines leave the left pole face, cross the gap (left → right) and re-enter the right pole, looping back around the outside. Hover any part for its name; click for an explanation. Drag to orbit.

plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates a Gouy balance apparatus used to measure magnetic susceptibility, showing a vertically suspended sample tube positioned between two cylindrical electromagnets and counterbalanced on a traditional beam balance against calibrated reference weights. The sample tube, labeled "Sample," hangs from one arm of the balance beam down into the gap between the two poles labeled "Electromagnets," while the opposite arm holds a pan carrying calibrated masses; the label "Magnetic field" with a line points to the region inside the gap, where curved purple arrows radiate outward in concentric arcs representing the inhomogeneous field lines diverging from the magnet poles. Because a paramagnetic sample containing unpaired electrons is drawn into the stronger-field region of the gap, it experiences a net downward force that makes it appear heavier, shifting the beam, while a diamagnetic sample with all electrons paired is weakly repelled and appears slightly lighter. The change in apparent mass — measured by adding or removing calibrated weights until the beam re-levels — is proportional to the number of unpaired electrons in the sample, providing a direct experimental count of those electrons. This figure introduces the Gouy balance as the key instrument for determining magnetic susceptibility and motivates its use to reveal that O2 possesses two unpaired electrons, a fact the Lewis-structure model fails to predict.

elements: Gold/brass balance stand: flat elliptical base disc on the floor, right of center
Vertical gold column rising from the base center
Gold pivot/fulcrum triangle at the top of the column
Horizontal gold balance beam resting on the fulcrum, extending far to the left and shorter to the right, with upturned hooked loops at both ends
Thin black suspension thread from the left beam hook down to the sample tube
Glass sample tube: narrow vertical cylinder with a flared lip/ring at the top and a rounded closed bottom
Blue liquid/solid sample column filling the lower two-thirds of the tube
Three black cords from the right beam hook down to the weighing pan
Shallow gold weighing pan (elliptical dish) on the right
Two or three small cylindrical calibrated metal weights sitting in the pan
Left electromagnet pole: horizontal steel cylinder pointing right toward the tube, with a raised collar/flange ring near its inner face
Right electromagnet pole: mirrored horizontal steel cylinder pointing left, with matching flange ring
Narrow air gap between the two pole faces, with the sample tube's lower portion hanging in it
Purple magnetic field lines: dense short arrows crossing the gap plus large concentric arcs bowing above and below the poles and fanning outward to the left and right
Arrowheads on the field lines showing direction (left pole -> right pole through the gap, returning around the outside)
Leader line and label 'Sample' pointing to the tube
Leader line and label 'Magnetic field' pointing to the arcs above the gap
V-shaped leader lines and label 'Electromagnets' below the two pole pieces
Susceptibility / apparent-mass readout panel (added for interaction)

interactions.teaches: A paramagnetic sample (unpaired electrons) is pulled INTO the high-field gap and reads heavier (χ > 0), while a diamagnetic sample (all electrons paired) is weakly pushed OUT and reads lighter (χ < 0) — the sign of the beam tilt is the sign of the susceptibility.
interactions.label: Sample

interactions.teaches: The apparent weight change grows with the square of the field, so beam deflection scales with B² while the measured susceptibility χ stays a constant property of the substance.
interactions.label: Magnet current → field B (T)

interactions.teaches: The measurement sequence: with the magnets off the beam is level, then as the field switches on the tube is drawn into (or pushed out of) the gap and the beam tips until counterweights restore balance.
interactions.label: Run the weighing procedure

interactions.teaches: Which part of the apparatus does what — beam, suspension, sample tube, pole pieces, field region, and counterweights — without cluttering the diagram with all labels at once.

demo_steps.title: Magnets off — beam level
demo_steps.narration: With no current in the electromagnets the tube feels only gravity. The counterweights exactly balance it and the beam sits horizontal: this is the zero-field reference mass.

demo_steps.title: Energize the field
demo_steps.narration: Current flows and purple field lines crowd the narrow gap. The paramagnetic sample is drawn down into the strongest part of the inhomogeneous field, so the left arm dips — the sample appears heavier.

demo_steps.title: Stronger field, larger pull
demo_steps.narration: Doubling the field roughly quadruples the force (F ∝ χB²). The deflection grows, but the susceptibility read out from the added counterweight is unchanged — it is a property of the substance, not of the magnet.

demo_steps.title: Swap in a diamagnetic sample
demo_steps.narration: With all electrons paired the sample is weakly expelled from the gap. The left arm rises instead of falling and χ flips sign, and the effect is far smaller than the paramagnetic case.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: total figure ~9 units wide × 8 units tall, origin at the magnet gap center. Stand: elliptical base disc radius 1.2, thickness 0.18, centered at (1.6, -3.3, 0); vertical column radius 0.13 from y=-3.3 to y=+3.9 at x=1.6; fulcrum a small gold triangle (0.35 wide, 0.4 tall) atop the column at y=+3.9. Balance beam: gold rod radius 0.07 running along X from x=-2.6 to x=+3.4 at y=+4.15, with upturned hook loops (radius 0.12) at both ends; beam rotates about the fulcrum at x=1.6, so the left arm is ~4.2 long and the right arm ~1.8 (left end hangs noticeably farther out, as in the source). Suspension: single black thread (0.02 radius) from the left hook straight down 1.1 units to the tube lip. Sample tube: glass cylinder radius 0.28, height 3.4, top lip ring radius 0.36, hemispherical bottom; tube top at y≈+2.9, bottom at y≈-0.6, centered at x=-2.6, so its lower half sits exactly in the magnet gap (gap center y≈+0.15). Blue sample fills the lower 65% of the tube. Right side: three black cords from the right hook fanning down 1.5 units to a shallow gold pan (elliptical dish, radius 0.75, depth 0.18) holding 2-3 short steel cylinders (radius 0.16, height 0.3). Electromagnets: two steel cylinders with axes along +X (screen-horizontal), each length 1.7 and radius 0.75, centered at y=+0.15, z=0; left pole spans x=-5.1 to -3.4, right pole spans x=-1.8 to -0.1; the 1.6-unit gap between the pole faces straddles the tube at x=-2.6. Each pole carries a raised collar ring (radius 0.82, width 0.25) just behind its inner face. Field lines: purple curves, ~14 short straight arrows spanning the gap left→right, plus 6 nested arcs bowing above the poles (rising to y≈+2.6) and 6 mirrored arcs below (dipping to y≈-2.2), plus outward fans of short arrows on the far left and far right pointing back toward the pole ends; arrowheads every ~0.6 units. Colors: stand/beam/pan gold #E4CE3B with darker edge #B39A22 and pale highlight #F5E98A; magnets steel gradient light #D9D9D9 → mid #9A9A9A → dark #5E5E5E with black outlines; tube glass pale cyan #CFE6E8 at 35% opacity with white rim highlight; sample blue #6B83E8 with a lighter top meniscus #93A9F2; field lines and arrowheads purple #8A3FD1; labels black sans-serif with black leader lines. Physics: force on sample F = (χ·A·B²)/(2μ₀); display apparent Δm ∝ χB², beam tilt angle = clamp(k·χ·B², ±9°), tilt DOWN on the tube side for χ>0. Use χ ≈ +1.5×10⁻³ (paramagnetic, e.g. 2 unpaired e⁻) and χ ≈ −2.0×10⁻⁵ (diamagnetic) so the diamagnetic deflection is visibly tiny (exaggerate ×20 for visibility but label it as exaggerated).
interactionPlan.notes: Build the balance beam, thread, tube, pan and weights as one THREE.Group pivoting about the fulcrum point so a single rotation.z drives the whole tilt; keep the tube vertical by counter-rotating its own group (a real balance's stirrup stays plumb). Glass tube = MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission 0.9, roughness 0.05, thickness 0.3, renderOrder after opaque geometry. Field lines as TubeGeometry along CatmullRomCurve3 arcs (radius 0.02) with small ConeGeometry arrowheads; drive their opacity and arrowhead scale from the fieldStrength slider (0 → invisible) and animate a subtle flow by offsetting a dashed texture or cycling arrowhead emissive. Magnets: CylinderGeometry rotated π/2 about Z, with a slight metalness 0.7 / roughness 0.35 and an outline pass (BackSide scaled mesh) to reproduce the ink-outlined cartoon look. Labels as CSS2DRenderer divs with thin leader lines drawn as Line geometry, shown on hover for partLabels; keep 'Sample', 'Magnetic field' and 'Electromagnets' pinned by default to match the source. Lighting: hemisphere light plus one key directional from upper-left to reproduce the source's left-lit shading. Readout panel (DOM overlay, top-right) shows B, sign and magnitude of χ, and Δm in mg. Animation timeline: 0-1 s field ramps in, 1-2 s beam tilts with an ease-out spring, 2-3 s counterweights added and beam returns to level with the readout locking in.

authoredContext:
Magnetic susceptibility measures the force experienced by a substance in a magnetic field. When we compare the weight of a sample to the weight measured in a magnetic field ( ), paramagnetic samples that are attracted to the magnet will appear heavier because of the force exerted by the magnetic field. We can calculate the number of unpaired electrons based on the increase in weight.

A Gouy balance compares the mass of a sample in the presence of a magnetic field with the mass with the electromagnet turned off to determine the number of unpaired electrons in a sample.

A diagram depicts a stand supporting two objects that are held in balance by a horizontal bar. On the right, the bar supports a dish that is holding two weights. On the left there is a line attached to a test tube labeled, “Sample tube.” The test tube has been lowered into the space labeled, “Magnetic field,” between two structures labeled, “Electromagnets.”

Experiments show that each O 2 molecule has two unpaired electrons. The Lewis-structure model does not predict the presence of these two unpaired electrons. Unlike oxygen, the apparent weight of most molecules decreases slightly in the presence of an inhomogeneous magnetic field. Materials in which all of the electrons are paired are diamagnetic and weakly repel a magnetic field. Paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials do not act as permanent magnets. Only in the presence of an applied magnetic field do they demonstrate attraction or repulsion.

discrepancies: Colors are noticeably darker than the source: the balance stand/beam/pan render as dull olive-brown rather than the bright yellow-gold of the original, and the electromagnet poles render as near-black/dark charcoal instead of the light silver-gray shaded cylinders.
The counterweights and pan on the right arm are very dark and tiny — in the source three bright steel weights sit clearly visible in a prominent gold dish; here they are barely discernible.

Field-line topology differs: the source shows elongated nested loops that hug the pole gap plus dense fringing arrow fans all along the top and bottom of both poles, while the generated version uses large near-circular concentric rings with fan arrows only at the far outer ends of the poles, so the strong-gradient crowding in the gap reads less clearly.

The sample tube is thinner/shorter relative to the magnet gap than in the source, and its blue column plus the glass lip are far less prominent (glass almost invisible), weakening the 'sample in the gap' reading.
The pole pieces in the source are drawn as two-stage cylinders with a clearly visible light collar ring; here the collars blend into the dark bodies and the pole faces barely read as distinct.
evaluation.notes: Composition, apparatus topology, labels and physics are all correct with an unusually rich and pedagogically apt interaction set (sample toggle, B slider, weighing procedure, guided steps), but the palette is significantly darker than the source — olive stand, near-black magnets, nearly invisible pan/weights — and the field-line pattern is more circular/sparser than the crowded gap loops of the original.
action_items: Brighten the gold material (raise color toward #E4CE3B/#F5E98A, lower metalness or add an emissive/ambient boost) and lighten the pole-piece steel to a light gray with a visible lighter collar so the magnets read as in the source.
Enlarge and lighten the weighing pan and counterweights so the three steel cylinders are clearly visible inside a bright gold dish.
Reshape the fringing field lines into elongated loops that hug the pole gap and add dense arrow fans along the top and bottom edges of both poles (as in the source) instead of only at the outer ends.
Increase the glass tube's visibility (stronger rim highlight, slightly larger radius) so the sample tube and its blue contents stand out against the field lines.

discrepancies: Field-line pattern differs substantially: the source shows a modest set of vertically elongated loops hugging the pole gap plus short fan arrows at the pole edges, while the generated figure draws ~14 large concentric ellipses that encircle both pole pieces and extend far beyond them, visually dominating the scene and overlapping the tube and poles.

Field arrow senses appear inverted relative to the source: in the original the arrows on the left of the assembly point up/outward and on the right point inward/down, whereas the generated left-side end-fan arrows point inward and the right-side arrows point outward.
Sample tube is noticeably shorter and the blue liquid column sits lower than in the source, where the tube extends well above the pole gap with the blue sample reaching up near the tube's top third.
Counterweights in the pan are much smaller and barely distinguishable; the source shows 3–4 clearly drawn steel cylinders sitting prominently in a dished pan.

The source's three suspension cords converge from a wide pan to a single hook; in the generated figure the pan/cord assembly is very small relative to the stand, making the right arm look under-scaled versus the left.
evaluation.notes: Composition, colors and labeling read clearly as the Gouy balance from the source, and the interaction set (sample toggle, B slider, weighing procedure, 4-step guided demo, hover explanations) is rich and pedagogically correct; the main weaknesses are an over-drawn, over-sized fringing-field pattern with partly reversed arrow senses, a shortened sample tube, and an under-scaled pan/weights.

discrepancies: Sample fill is inverted: the source shows the blue sample occupying the UPPER portion of the tube (so it spans the field boundary, which is the point of the Gouy method), while the generated tube is filled from the bottom up to ~68%.

Field-line pattern is coarser than the source: fewer nested fringing arcs, and the outer 'end fans' render as isolated floating arrow pairs at the far left/right with no connecting arcs, which reads as stray marks rather than flux lines.

Pole/gap proportions differ — the source shows two large cylinders separated by a narrow gap barely wider than the tube; the generated gap is noticeably wide relative to pole diameter, weakening the 'field crowded in the gap' impression.

The dense gap hatching (the tight zig-zag of short field lines between the pole faces in the source) is reduced to two short arrow stubs per row, so the strong-field region is less visually emphasized.

Beam/stand proportions: the source beam is longer and the tube hangs from a point well clear of the magnet assembly; in the generated figure the left hook sits almost directly over the pole gap, slightly compressing the composition.
